sections.heading: What is the Tree DFS Pattern?
sections.content: Tree DFS (Depth-First Search) explores a tree by going as deep as possible down one branch before backing up and trying the next. It is usually written with recursion, where the call stack remembers the path, or with an explicit stack. DFS is the natural tool for questions about paths, subtrees, depths and heights, because the answer for a node depends on the answers for its children. It runs in O(n) time and O(h) space, where h is the height of the tree.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Root-to-leaf or any-to-any path problems (path sum, all paths, maximum path)
Subtree properties: height, diameter, balance, symmetry, equality
Validate or compare trees (same tree, subtree, mirror)
Lowest common ancestor and ancestor-descendant questions
Building or modifying trees (invert, flatten, construct from traversals)
Counting or collecting nodes that satisfy a condition along the path
Backtracking over tree paths
Keywords: path, subtree, height, depth, diameter, ancestor, root to leaf, balanced, symmetric

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Picture walking through a maze of corridors that fork in two. DFS picks a corridor and follows it all the way to a dead end, then returns to the last fork and takes the other branch. The only difference between preorder, inorder and postorder is when you do your work at a node: before visiting the children, between them, or after both are done.

The DFS Recipe for Tree Problems
items: 1. Base case: what should a null node return (0, true, null, empty list)?
2. Decide what each node needs to know: from ancestors (parameters) or from children (return value)?
3. Decide what to return from a call (height, sum, boolean, node)
4. Combine the left and right results at the current node
5. If the answer is not what you return (diameter, max path), update a variable outside the recursion
6. Leaf check is node.left == null && node.right == null, not just node == null

Example 2: Same Tree and Symmetric Tree
sections.code:
fun isSameTree(p: TreeNode?, q: TreeNode?): Boolean {
    if (p == null && q == null) return true
    if (p == null || q == null) return false
    return p.`val` == q.`val` &&
        isSameTree(p.left, q.left) &&
        isSameTree(p.right, q.right)
}

fun isSymmetric(root: TreeNode?): Boolean =
    root == null || isMirror(root.left, root.right)

fun isMirror(a: TreeNode?, b: TreeNode?): Boolean {
    if (a == null && b == null) return true
    if (a == null || b == null) return false
    return a.`val` == b.`val` &&
        isMirror(a.left, b.right) &&              // outer pair
        isMirror(a.right, b.left)                 // inner pair
}
// Time: O(n)   Space: O(h)

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Treating a node with one child as a leaf (a leaf has both children null)
Forgetting the base case for null, which causes a NullPointerException
Not backtracking (removing the last element from the path) after exploring a branch
Adding the same path list to the result instead of copying it (ArrayList(path))
Returning the diameter or max path sum instead of the height or gain, and updating a variable separately
Not ignoring negative branches in the maximum path sum problem
Recomputing heights from every node, which gives O(n²) instead of O(n)
Overflowing the call stack on very deep trees (use an iterative version)
Mixing up preorder, inorder and postorder when building or serializing a tree

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: DFS goes deep first and is usually written with recursion
Preorder works on the node before the children, inorder between them, postorder after them
Pass information down for top-down problems and return information up for bottom-up problems
When the answer is not the return value (diameter, max path sum), track it in an outer variable
A leaf has no left and no right child, so check both
Time is O(n) and space is O(h), where h is the tree height
